design_detail: Single-author narrative review, published under the journal's 'Basel Proceedings' heading, by an author from the Clinical Biology Laboratory of Ghent University Hospital, summarizing published detection times of amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDMA and related drugs, cannabis, cocaine, LSD, heroin and morphine, flunitrazepam (after a single dose) and GHB in blood (serum or plasma), urine and oral fluid, with a short section on hair. Tables 1-3 give one 'typical' study per drug and fluid (dose and route given, analyte, cutoff, detection time, reference) and Table 2 adds maximal detection times in urine. The author says the times are based as far as possible on the methods' limits of detection or quantification rather than on cutoffs. No search methods, selection criteria or appraisal of the cited studies; the sources are controlled administration studies, often in one to a few volunteers and, as the author notes, at doses low compared with street use, studies of people forced to stop chronic use in prison or detoxification, and for several table entries a 1994 compendium of data sheets from the Institute of Legal Medicine of the University of Zürich. Doses appear on this card only as the conditions of the cited studies; the review's statements on usual doses are not extracted.
can_establish: The ranges of detection times reported in the studies the author chose, by drug, body fluid, analyte and analytical limit, and the factors the author lists as determining detection time.
cannot_establish: The detection time for a particular person, amount or test (many entries rest on one study of one or two volunteers, at laboratory detection limits rather than the cutoffs used in screening), the completeness of the evidence (no search), or detection times for drugs it does not cover (benzodiazepines other than flunitrazepam, prescription opioids other than morphine and codeine, ketamine, newer substances).

sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the author. One study per drug and fluid is put in each table as 'typical'.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by one author. Controlled-administration studies give single, often low doses to few volunteers (the author says doses are relatively low compared with street doses, p. 200), while the longest times come from people stopping heavy use in prison or detoxification; the tables show one study per cell, so the spread between these extremes is not visible.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; the cited studies used controlled administration or studied people who had stopped chronic use (p. 200, Abstract and Introduction).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the cited studies; the detoxification-ward study (Reiter et al., 2001, cited as the Lübeck study) gives cannabis, cocaine and opiate results from the same 52 people without saying how many used each drug.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: In the studies of people who stopped (prison, detoxification ward, a closed research unit), times are from admission or from reported last use; supervision is described as incomplete in one cannabis study (p. 203).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (descriptive summary of detection times).

outcomes.instruments: Cited methods: immunoassays (EMIT, ELISA, EIA, FPIA, RIA), GC-MS, GC-MS-MS, LC-MS, GC-MS with negative chemical ionization, liquid chromatography with diode-array detection, at limits of detection or quantification or at stated cutoffs.
outcomes.validity_norms: The author states that times in Tables 1-3 are based as much as possible on limits of quantification or detection rather than cutoffs (p. 200), which gives longer times than screening cutoffs would; some table entries nevertheless use cutoffs (for example 1000 ng/mL for benzoylecgonine and 10,000 ng/mL for GHB in Table 2).
outcomes.operationalization: Detection time: time after a dose (or after stopping, or after admission) during which the drug or metabolite could be measured above the stated limit or cutoff; 'maximal detection time' in Table 2 is the longest reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, single values or ranges per study (see key findings); no pooling, intervals or measures of spread beyond those printed in the cited studies.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection of one 'typical' study per table cell; the conclusion's general figures (blood 1-2 days, oral fluid 5-48 hours, urine 1.5-4 days after a single dose and about 1 week after chronic use) are summaries of these selections, not estimates from a defined body of studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A compilation of detection times from selected studies, mostly single controlled doses in few volunteers measured at laboratory detection limits, plus a few studies of people who stopped heavy use; the times vary widely with dose, analyte, fluid and analytical limit, and some entries contradict the text.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion turn these into general rules: in blood most drugs detectable for 1 or 2 days, in urine 1.5 to 4 days after a single dose and about 1 week after chronic use, longer in extreme cases of cocaine (22 days) and cannabis (up to 3 months) use, and in oral fluid 5-48 hours (pp. 200, 204). The conclusion also says detection times are extremely variable and that many factors remain unknown (p. 204), which the rules in the abstract do not convey; the abstract and conclusion give the flunitrazepam dose as 1 or 2 ng where the body describes 1 and 2 mg.

timeline.event: The author's own earlier review of detection times in urine (Vandevenne, Vandenbussche & Verstraete, 2000), cited for the list of factors that determine detection time (p. 200); not read.

Monitored-abstinence study of 60 people who used cannabis regularly: last positive urine screen (50 ng/mL) up to 29.8 days after admission, 13 of 20 with the highest initial levels still positive on their last day of observation
Clinical review of urine drug tests that cites this review among the nine sources of its table of approximate urine detection times (PDF p. 4)

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited summary whose figures are second-hand and rest on few, small studies; for cannabis, the monitored-abstinence data of Goodwin et al. (2008) and the 2017 clinical review give later accounts of urine detection after regular use.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author from the Clinical Biology Laboratory, Ghent University Hospital, Belgium (p. 200); the Basel meeting behind the proceedings is not described in the article. Two of the 56 references are the author's own earlier reviews (detection times in urine; analysis of drugs in saliva).

what_would_settle_it: A systematic synthesis of controlled-dosing and monitored-abstinence studies, by drug, body fluid and cutoff (including the cutoffs used in workplace, roadside and treatment testing), in people with occasional and with heavy use, with time since last use known and follow-up long enough that the last positive result is observed.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; one study per drug and fluid chosen by the author as typical.

No formal appraisal; the author notes that controlled doses are low compared with street doses (p. 200) and that subjects in one cannabis study were not supervised throughout (p. 203), but sample sizes and methods of the cited studies are mostly not given.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of 56 references are the author's own reviews, used for the list of factors and for oral-fluid times of heroin and morphine; the data come mostly from others.
Mostly reported data with references; the longest cannabis reports are labelled probably exceptional.

domains.domain: Balance of single-dose laboratory data against data from people who stopped heavy use
domains.note: The 'typical' times come mostly from single controlled doses, the maxima from people stopping heavy use; the review says so, but shows few data between these extremes.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is a useful map of what had been measured by 2004 and is candid about variability, but its selection is unsystematic, each table cell rests on one study (sometimes of one or two volunteers), detection limits and cutoffs are mixed, and several entries contradict the text. It may be cited, as second-hand figures, for the factors that determine detection time, for the general ordering of fluids (hair, then urine, sweat, oral fluid and blood), and for specific detection times as the reported results of named studies with their analyte, limit and conditions. It should not be cited for the detection time of a given person or test, and claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: The author's summary: at low nanogram-per-millilitre limits, most drugs are detectable in blood for 1 or 2 days and in oral fluid for 5-48 hours; in urine, a single dose is detectable for 1.5 to 4 days, and after chronic use for about 1 week after the last use, in extreme cases longer for cocaine (22 days) and cannabis (up to 3 months); GHB is detectable for a much shorter time; detection time is generally longest in hair, then urine, sweat, oral fluid and blood.

Detection time depends on the amount taken, the preparation and route, acute versus chronic use, the body fluid tested, the detection limit or cutoff of the method, the molecule or metabolite sought, the pH and concentration of urine or oral fluid, and individual differences in metabolism (and, in the abstract, renal clearance); detection is longer with the most sensitive methods and the longest-persisting metabolite.

Sources and their limits: the data come from controlled administration to volunteers, usually at doses the author calls low compared with street doses, or from people forced to stop (often chronic) use in prison or detoxification, which gives no information on a single dose; the tables use limits of detection or quantification as far as possible, not screening cutoffs.

Amphetamine: half-life 7 to 34 hours depending on urinary pH (about 30% excreted unchanged at normal pH, up to 74% at pH 5); urine detection after a single intake generally accepted as 1-3 days; in a controlled study the share of urine samples screening positive (cutoff above 1000 ng/mL) was 19%, 67% and 88% after 5, 10 and 20 mg (study conditions); in people entering prison, detection lasted 4.8 days on average and almost 9 days at most; oral fluid 20 to 50 hours (LOD 10 ng/mL).
key_findings.locator: Amphetamine, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 201, maximal 9 days); Table 3 (p. 202)

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine in urine after a single controlled oral dose of 10 mg (study condition): last detection 87.2 ± 51 hours (range 46-144) at the limit of quantification (2.5 ng/mL), 42.7 ± 22.8 hours (22-65) at cutoffs of 500 ng/mL methamphetamine and 200 ng/mL amphetamine, and 51.6 ± 26.3 hours (25-77) at half those cutoffs; after smoking 22 mg, urine about 300 ng/mL for 60 hours and blood about 3 ng/mL for 48 hours; half-life 10 to 30 hours.

Methamphetamine in oral fluid: detectable for at least 24 hours after 10 mg sustained-release (mean 18.8 ng/mL) and for 36-72 hours after 4 doses of 10 or 20 mg (study conditions); oral-fluid concentrations were 2.3 to 4.3 times plasma, and the collection method changed them (neutral cotton swabs 1.47 times citric-acid swabs and 1.31 times sour-candy stimulation; neutral Salivette 1.92 times sour candy).

MDMA: in 2 volunteers given 100 mg (study condition), detectable in blood (20 ng/mL) for 24 hours and in urine for more than 48 hours; urine detection generally accepted as 1-3 days; 24 hours after 100 mg in 8 people, 13.5 (SD 18.6) ng/mL in blood and 126.2 (SD 101.8) ng/mL in unstimulated oral fluid, about 10 times higher; MDEA 1.4-2.6 days in urine; MBDB 36 hours in urine and 17 hours in oral fluid.
key_findings.locator: Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA, Ecstasy) and Derivatives, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cannabis pharmacokinetics: plasma THC peaks within about 3-8 minutes of smoking and falls quickly (half-life about 30 minutes); the metabolite THCCOOH has a half-life of about 20-57 hours with occasional use and 3-13 days with regular use; THC itself is detectable for about 5 hours in plasma (LOD 1 ng/mL) and 10 hours in urine (LOD 10 ng/mL).

Cannabis in urine after a single smoked cigarette (study conditions): last positive (THCCOOH 15 ng/mL by GC-MS) at 33.7 ± 9.2 hours (1.75% THC) and 88.6 ± 9.5 hours (3.55% THC); positive by EMIT (cutoff above 20 ng/mL) for 2.1 and 3.8 days; in another study, last positive 42 ± 10 hours (range 2-72) by EIA and 58 ± 6 hours (16-72) by GC-MS, in subjects not supervised throughout; after eating two brownies with 2.8% THC, positive by EMIT (20 ng/mL) for 5.9 days.
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives 3.50% and 87 hours for the second cigarette (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cannabis after stopping regular use: in chronic use THCCOOH can be detected in urine for weeks or even months; in 52 people admitted to a detoxification ward (Reiter et al., 2001, cited as the Lübeck study) urine THCCOOH (LOD 10 ng/mL) stayed detectable for 4.9 days on average and 18 days at most, and serum THCCOOH for 23.8 hours on average and 49 hours at most; the longest reported urine detection times, 93 and 95 days, are probably exceptional cases.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 201, maximal 95 days)

key_findings.finding: Cannabis in oral fluid: after smoked or oral cannabis, THC was positive in all analyses for up to 15 hours (range 1-24) by ELISA and 13 hours (1-24) by GC-MS-MS, with the last positive sample at 31 hours (1-72) and 34 hours (1-72); creatinine normalization smooths urine THCCOOH curves but considerable variation between consecutive specimens remains.

Cocaine: in blood 4-6 hours after 20 mg and 12 hours after 100 mg (study conditions); benzoylecgonine in urine 1-2 days after 20 mg intravenously and 2-3 days after 1.5 mg/kg intranasally; in serum of people who used chronically, benzoylecgonine (LOD 25 ng/mL) 5.1 days on average and 8.6 at most; in oral fluid cocaine 5-12 hours and benzoylecgonine 12-24 hours after a single dose (1 ng/mL methods), up to 10 days with chronic use (LOD 0.5 ng/mL).

Cocaine after stopping: in 18 people housed for up to 14 days on a closed research unit (FPIA, cutoff 300 ng/mL benzoylecgonine equivalents), the first negative specimen came 43.6 ± 17.1 hours (16-66) and the last positive 57.5 ± 31.6 hours (11-147) after admission, or 81 ± 34 hours (34-162) after the last reported use; in the detoxification-ward study, benzoylecgonine (LOD 50 ng/mL) was detectable for 47.4 hours on average and 4.9 days at most; in people using cocaine heavily, benzoylecgonine has been detected 22 days after the last use.
After cocaine used as a topical anaesthetic in nasal surgery, benzoylecgonine was positive in all subjects at 24 hours and negative in all samples at 72 hours.

Heroin and morphine: half-lives about 2-7 minutes (heroin), 6-25 minutes (6-acetylmorphine) and 2-3 hours (morphine); after 3, 6 and 12 mg heroin intravenously, 6-acetylmorphine was detectable in urine for 2.3, 2.6 and 4.5 hours and total morphine (LOD 300 ng/mL) for 18.5, 24.8 and 35.3 hours; after 10-15 mg, total morphine for 11-54 hours (study conditions); in the detoxification-ward study, 6-acetylmorphine (LOD 10 ng/mL) 5 hours on average (at most 34.5 hours) and total morphine (LOD 25 ng/mL) 4.95 days (at most 11.3 days).
key_findings.locator: Opiates: Heroin and Morphine, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 201, maximal 11.3 days)

key_findings.finding: In 63 men dependent on heroin, urine morphine by immunoassay was positive in 88.4% after 1 day, 74.2% after 2, 64.2% after 3, 57.1% after 4, 63.3% after 5 and 44.8% after 6 days.
key_findings.note: The percentages are not monotonic (day 5 above day 4), suggesting changing denominators; numbers per day are not given.

key_findings.finding: Opioids in blood and oral fluid: morphine in blood (LOD 1 ng/mL) for 20 hours after 12 or 20 mg heroin intravenously and 12 hours after 9 mg intranasally; in blood of people who used chronically, total morphine 29.2 hours and free morphine 14.4 hours on average (both at most 5 days); in oral fluid 6-acetylmorphine 0.5-8 hours and morphine 12-24 hours; codeine in oral fluid 21 hours at a 2.5 ng/mL cutoff and 7 hours at 40 ng/mL after 60 or 120 mg (study conditions).
key_findings.locator: Opiates: Heroin and Morphine, 2nd paragraph (p. 203) and 4th paragraph (p. 204)

key_findings.finding: LSD: plasma LSD fell below the limit of detection (5 pg/mL) 24 and 48 hours after a dose; only 1% is excreted unchanged; LSD is detectable in urine for about 24 hours after a typical dose and at most 80 hours (RIA, 100 pg/mL cutoff); urine LSD fell below 200 pg/mL within 36 hours; the metabolite 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-LSD, at a mean of 42.9 times (median 16.1) the LSD concentration, was detectable for up to 96 hours.

Flunitrazepam after a single dose: with GC-MS in negative chemical ionization (LOD 10 pg/mL), 7-aminoflunitrazepam was detected in urine for 14 days in 6, 21 days in 1 and 28 days in 3 of 10 people given 2 mg (study condition); after 1 mg, detection lasted 48 to 120 hours depending on the method, and immunoassays never gave a positive result; in oral fluid detection did not exceed 6 hours.
key_findings.locator: Flunitrazepam: Detection Time after a Single Intake, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: GHB: half-life about 20 minutes; because the body makes it, thresholds are needed (proposed: 5 µg/mL in blood, 50 µg/mL in post-mortem blood, 10 µg/mL in urine, 2 ng/mg in hair); detectable for about 5 hours in blood and oral fluid and under 12 hours in urine; a sweat patch still showed raised levels 12 or 24 hours later.

Hair: detection depends on hair length (growth 0.8-1.3 cm a month); few data on single doses: a single 2 mg flunitrazepam dose was detectable, a 3 mg clonazepam dose was found in 6 of 10 people, about one cannabis joint a week corresponded to 0.02-3 ng/mg, and one MDMA tablet to about 0.5 ng/mg but was not detectable in some people.
key_findings.locator: Minimal Detectable Amounts in Hair, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the conclusion give the flunitrazepam dose as 1 or 2 ng; the body describes doses of 2 mg and 1 mg.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unit error in the summary sentences; the body's mg values are the conditions of the cited studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Amphetamine in blood: the text says detectable for 46 hours after 10 mg (p. 200), while Table 1 gives 6 mg orally for the same reference (8) and the same 46 hours (p. 201).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose behind the 46-hour figure is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Cannabis in urine after a single cigarette: the text gives 3.55% THC and a last positive at 88.6 ± 9.5 hours (p. 202), Table 2 gives 3.50% and 87 hours (p. 201), and a later sentence on the same reference speaks of 3.5% (p. 202).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote the text's value with its spread and note the table's.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 126 ng/mL as the cutoff for MDMA in oral fluid, the same figure as the mean concentration measured 24 hours after 100 mg in the text (126.2 ng/mL).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table's cutoff for MDMA in oral fluid is probably a concentration entered in the wrong column; the detection limit behind the 24 hours is not given.

reporting_issues.issue: THC in plasma: the text gives detection for about 5 hours at an LOD of 1 ng/mL (p. 202), while Table 1 gives 5 hours at a cutoff of 10 ng/mL (p. 201); a detection time of 25 days for THCCOOH (LOD 5 ng/mL) from the reference behind Table 1 is given without saying in which fluid (p. 202), while Table 1 gives 36 hours in blood.
reporting_issues.consequence: The analytical limits and fluid behind these cannabis blood figures are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: In the closed-unit cocaine study, the same mean, 88.4 hours, is given for the time to the first negative and to the last positive after creatinine normalization, with different SDs and ranges (20.7, 20-100; 51.0, 35.6-235).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is probably a transcription error; check the primary paper (Preston et al., 2002) before citing the normalized figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the tables are based as far as possible on limits of detection or quantification rather than cutoffs (p. 200), but several entries use cutoffs (Table 2: benzoylecgonine 1000 ng/mL, GHB 10,000 ng/mL; Table 3: GHB 4000 ng/mL), the heroin entry in Table 2 gives no limit, and each 'typical' value rests on a single study, sometimes of one or two people.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rows are not comparable with each other, and LOD-based times run longer than a screening test at a standard cutoff would show.

reporting_issues.issue: One smoked methamphetamine study (reference 13) is described as using methamphetamine hydrochloride for the blood result and methamphetamine base for the urine result.
